breakdown.understanding:
Read as 15 findings, but they are not 15 pieces: three pairs are the same defect filed twice (weekly-end-date.test.ts appears at positions 1 and 6; the two text-operator findings at 3 and 13 contradict each other on whether fetched money is being dropped; the two ReDoS findings at 5 and 12 disagree on whether it belongs in this diff at all), two are about PR #9's metadata and are un-actionable now it is merged, and the rest cluster into six seams. I re-checked every one against main rather than trusting the ticket: the duplicated test file, both literal `.includes` sites, the unguarded `likePatternToRegex` call, the `box.x > 850` threshold, both needless exports, the `// ? added here` scar, the duplicated e2e helpers and the three `id: ""` categories all still reproduce. Nothing was dropped as no-longer-true.

Adjacent pairs, one line each:

**Sankey + Budget Analysis (clubbed into one issue).** Same four-line change at two call sites of the same helper, two files plus their existing test files, well under the 6-file budget. Neither site has meaning until the other is fixed — the defect a user sees is 'the same filter text answers differently in different reports', and fixing one site leaves that exactly as true. Clubbed, with AC-1..AC-3 for Sankey and AC-4..AC-6 for Budget Analysis.

**The ReDoS bound + the module's surface (clubbed into one issue).** likePattern.ts and budgetDataQuery.ts, and piece 7 has no user-facing meaning of its own — unexporting a constant and deleting a stale comment are invisible until someone edits those same two files. Combined size is 3 files. The `canNarrowAxisByConditions` half is a real judgement call (drop the export, or test it directly) and is written as its own acceptance line rather than being decided for the planner. Clubbed.

**ReDoS bound (piece 2) ↔ text-operator routing (piece 1): kept split.** Piece 1 consumes the helper; piece 2 changes the helper. Different risks — one is wrong totals, one is a hung render thread — and both are independently shippable. Preference, not dependency: landing the bound first means the two new call sites inherit the wildcard cap on arrival, and landing the routing first leaves two more sites briefly unguarded. Neither *cannot* be built before the other, so no `depends_on`; this is the only ordering preference in the split and it lives here rather than in the issue graph.

**ReDoS bound ↔ e2e selector work: kept split.** loot-core's shared pattern module and the desktop client's e2e page model share no file and no reviewer. Trivially independent.

**e2e selector + e2e helper duplication (clubbed into one issue).** custom-report-page.ts and reports.test.ts are the same e2e suite added by PR #9, the page model is the consumer of the helpers, and the helper hoist on its own has nothing to show — no behaviour changes, no user sees it. Combined 3 files. The two faces are named in the context because one of them (the stable hook) has an accessibility consequence the review did not mention and the other does not.

**e2e suite ↔ weekly-end-date.test.ts: kept split.** Different runners (Playwright vs Vitest), different files, and piece 4 is a deletion decision that needs both 338-line and 1100-line files read against each other before anyone can say what it uniquely adds. That reading is the work; it does not fit inside the previous piece.

**weekly-end-date.test.ts ↔ React duplicate keys: kept split.** A test-file deletion and a production render fix. No shared file.

**React keys ↔ release note: kept split.** One production file plus its consumers, versus one markdown file. No shared file, no shared reviewer.

Two findings are deferred rather than split: PR #9's title and body. The PR is merged, and the roadmap already records that the twelve `gh pr edit --title` calls it would take are a person's decision and not a ticket's — #75 is the canonical home for the `[AI]` prefix finding, and #75 is currently parked behind a label that does not apply to it. Filing them again here would race it.

No `epic_links`. The other open epics are #41 (schedule occurrences) and #14 (weekly report end-date). Piece 4 touches a file named after #14's subject matter, but it is a merge leftover from PR #9 and nothing about #14's product — the end-date helper, whose children #20 and #21 have both closed — has to exist first. Neither edge is 'cannot be built yet'.

No `covers` anywhere: `spec.paths` names `docs/spec` and `SPEC.md`, and the roadmap records that neither exists. There are no TR- ids to claim.

pieces.title: A category text filter means the same thing in Sankey and Budget Analysis as in Custom and Grouped
pieces.why: A person who types a category filter containing `%` or `?` into a Sankey report or a Budget Analysis report gets a different answer than the same filter gives in a Custom or Grouped report. In Budget Analysis the filtered list decides which categories get a cell in the grid, so the report's totals are made of a different set than the one the user asked for.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, four files. What a person sees: the Sankey report and the Budget Analysis report in Reports, each filtered on a category or category-group text condition. What the contract is: both sites consume `likePatternToRegex` and `getNormalisedString` from `@actual-app/core/shared`, a contract `budgetDataQuery.ts` already established — this slice conforms to it, it does not define it.

Neither site discards fetched money today, and the acceptance below does not claim it does. `filterCategoryGroups` in sankey-spreadsheet.ts has one caller, and its data comes from `api/budget-month` with no conditions passed; budget-analysis-spreadsheet.ts sums `envelope-budget-month`, likewise unconditioned. The comment at sankey-spreadsheet.ts:425-428 says so explicitly. The user-visible defect is that the reports answer a different question from the one the user asked, and that they disagree with the Custom and Grouped reports about what `%` means.

The reference implementation to copy is budgetDataQuery.ts:246-265, including its comments explaining why `matches` is deliberately *not* routed through `likePatternToRegex` and why the `$notlike` `OR IS NULL` disjunct never fires for a category name. Both existing test files (`sankey-spreadsheet.test.ts`, `budget-analysis-spreadsheet.test.ts`) already exist; extend them rather than adding new files.

The epic filed this twice with contradictory severity — once as money being dropped, once as a mere inconsistency. I have taken the second reading, which the code supports, and said so rather than splitting the difference.
acceptance: **AC-1** On the Sankey report, a category text filter of `contains "%"` renders a node for every category the query returned, and `contains "o%"` renders the categories whose name contains an `o` — the same set a Custom report with the same condition returns, not an empty chart.
**AC-2** On the Sankey report, `doesNotContain` is the exact negation of `contains` at the same value, and neither operator reads the value as a literal substring.

**AC-3** `sankey-spreadsheet.test.ts` gains the differential cases: the filter value is interpreted identically by the report and by the query that fed it, checked for `%`, `?` and a mixed value such as `o%`, at both sites' existing fixtures.

**AC-4** On the Budget Analysis report, a category text filter of `contains "%"` produces a per-month category list that is the full set the month data contains, and every one of those categories gets a cell in the analysis grid.

**AC-5** On the Budget Analysis report, a mixed value such as `o%` matches the categories whose name contains an `o`, and the grid's totals are computed from that same list — a category excluded from the grid is not silently present in the totals.
**AC-6** `budget-analysis-spreadsheet.test.ts` gains the same differential cases as AC-3, against the same values.
**AC-7** A category filter value with no wildcard in it behaves exactly as it does today: no existing report's rows, cells or totals change for `is`, `oneOf`, `notOneOf` or an ordinary substring.
pieces.risk: Budget Analysis decides which categories reach the grid and therefore what the totals are made of, so a routing mistake here moves money between totals rather than merely hiding a row. The bound direction matters: the filter must never become stricter than the query, or categories the query fetched will drop out of the grid. Test the wildcard values explicitly — the ordinary-substring case is the one that passes by accident.
out_of_scope: Changing `matches`, which compiles to `$regexp` and is deliberately not a LIKE pattern; budgetDataQuery.ts:267-284 already documents why.
Changing the query side, `UNICODE_LIKE`, or rule evaluation.
The age-of-money report's text operators, which are a separate implementation at age-of-money-spreadsheet.ts:341-393 and were not reported.
Bounding the pattern's wildcard count or length — that is the ReDoS piece and it changes `likePatternToRegex` itself.

pieces.title: A wildcard-heavy filter value cannot hang a report, and the shared pattern module stops exporting what nothing uses
pieces.why: A person who types a category filter such as `%%%%%%Z` into a Custom or Grouped report today blocks the browser's main thread for minutes on a budget with a few hundred categories, because the value is compiled into an unbounded regex once per category per condition. After this, the report renders immediately.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, three files. What a person sees: the Custom and Grouped report, filtering a category axis by a text value containing several `%`. What the contract is: this slice *defines* the bound on `likePatternToRegex` in `@actual-app/core/shared`, and every LIKE-pattern consumer inherits it — `unicodeLike.ts` (which already memoises through an LRU) and the report axis path both go through the same function.

The measured shape from the epic: 3 `%` costs 3ms per category, 4 costs 21ms, 5 costs 150ms, 6 costs 850ms, and the axis predicate runs once per category per condition on every render. Recompilation is not the cost — 200 compiles of one pattern total under a millisecond — so memoising alone buys nothing and the bound is the fix. The epic filed this twice: once as a report hang, once as explicitly not-this-diff. I am treating it as in scope because it is a live hang on `main` today, and I have said so rather than silently re-ranking it.

The dangerous half is the direction of the bound. If the bound rejects an over-long or over-wildcarded value by returning false, the axis becomes *narrower* than the query's result set, and a category the query fetched silently loses its money from every total — the exact defect class the Custom and Grouped reports were fixed for in PR #9. The bound must fail open: a rejected value keeps every category, the same shape `matches` already uses at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278 when its 256-character test fails. Say which you chose and why in the code.

The three export/comment findings travel with the behaviour change because they are the same two files and none of them is visible until someone edits them: `REGEX_SPECIAL` (likePattern.ts:14) has no consumer outside its own module, `canNarrowAxisByConditions` (budgetDataQuery.ts:89) is exported and called once from line 137 of the same file, and line 25 ends `// ? added here`, a review scar carried into the file that declares itself the single definition of the pattern language.
acceptance: **AC-1** Typing a category filter value of six or more `%` characters into a Custom report's category axis renders the report in the same time as an ordinary value — under a second on a budget with several hundred categories — where it currently blocks the main thread for minutes.

**AC-2** The bound lives inside `likePatternToRegex`, so every LIKE-pattern consumer inherits it: the report axis path and the sqlite `UNICODE_LIKE` path are both covered by one change and one test, not two.

**AC-3** An over-long or over-wildcarded value is rejected *openly*: the axis keeps every category rather than dropping the ones the query returned, so no money leaves a total because the value was too long. This is asserted directly, with a value the bound refuses, by showing the axis still carries the full category set.
**AC-4** An ordinary value with no wildcard and no unusual length filters the category axis exactly as it does today — the bound rejects nothing a user would plausibly type.
**AC-5** `REGEX_SPECIAL` is no longer exported from `@actual-app/core/shared/likePattern`, and nothing outside that module imported it.

**AC-6** `canNarrowAxisByConditions` is either unexported or covered by a direct test of its own — it is the gate that decides whether narrowing the axis is sound at all, so whichever of the two you choose, the reason is written next to it.
**AC-7** The trailing `// ? added here` comment is gone from the escaped-wildcard branch of `likePatternToRegex`.
pieces.risk: The bound is on the render path for every report that narrows a category axis, and its failure direction is the money-losing one: a bound that rejects too eagerly drops categories the query fetched and their money with them. AC-3 exists because that is the mistake this piece can make, and it must be proven, not assumed. The export removals are safe only if the consumers really are zero — verify, do not assume.
out_of_scope: Re-measuring or bounding main's pre-existing per-transaction `matches` regex on the query side, which the epic notes is already slow and is larger there; that is a separate change to `aql/compiler.ts`.
Routing the Sankey and Budget Analysis reports through the shared pattern — that is the text-operator piece.
Any memoisation whose only purpose is to avoid recompiling, which the measurements say is not the cost.

pieces.title: The custom report's filter button can be found without knowing the viewport width
pieces.why: The custom report e2e suite finds the filter button by scanning for an unnamed button whose x-coordinate exceeds 850. Change the viewport or let the toolbar reflow and the locator silently resolves to nothing: the conditions-menu scenarios skip, then fail further down with an unrelated message. The button also carries no accessible name, so a screen-reader user cannot find it either.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, three files. What a person sees: the Custom report toolbar, and the compact icon-only filter button the e2e suite has to open. What the contract is: no new contract; this slice gives an existing component a stable hook and consumes it.

`openConditionsMenu` in packages/desktop-client/e2e/page-models/custom-report-page.ts:55-77 selects all buttons with no accessible name and keeps the first whose bounding box sits right of x=850. The button it wants is `CompactFiltersButton`, rendered by `FilterButton` in FiltersMenu.tsx:752-758 when `compact` is set — which ReportTopbar.tsx:234-235 does. `CompactFiltersButton` renders an `SvgFilter` and nothing else, so it has no accessible name today; the sibling non-compact `FiltersButton` at least renders the word Filter.

Prefer a hook a person benefits from over a hook only a test can see: an accessible name or a `title` on the compact button fixes the screen-reader case and gives the locator something stable at the same time. `data-testid` is acceptable if no name can be given, but say why.

The second half of this issue is the e2e file's own duplication: `selectOnlyBillsGroup` is byte-identical at reports.test.ts:311 and :479, and `switchToAnyOf` at :343 and :501 differs only by a two-line comment. Both close over only `page` and `customReportPage`, and both blocks sit inside the enclosing `custom reports` describe, so one hoisted copy serves both. Keep the more informative comment on the survivor.

**Risk.** `verify.e2e` is empty in `.sdlc/config.yml`, so no CI check runs these 22 files. The regression guard here is real only when someone runs `yarn e2e` locally — that is a fact worth stating in the PR rather than discovering later.
acceptance: **AC-1** `openConditionsMenu` locates the filter button by a stable hook — an accessible name, a `title`, or a test id — and contains no coordinate comparison; no `boundingBox().x` threshold remains in the page model.
**AC-2** The button carries that hook in the compact form the custom report toolbar renders, so the locator does not depend on the non-compact variant also being on the page.

**AC-3** The hook is one a person benefits from: the compact filter button has an accessible name, so a screen reader announces it. If a test id is used instead because no name can be given, the reason is written next to it.
**AC-4** When the button cannot be found the page model throws as it does today — the failure stays loud rather than becoming a skipped menu scenario.
**AC-5** `selectOnlyBillsGroup` and `switchToAnyOf` each exist once in reports.test.ts, hoisted to the enclosing `custom reports` describe, with the more informative comment kept on the survivor.
**AC-6** The custom-report e2e suite runs green at Playwright's default 1280px viewport and at a narrower one, with no test relying on where the button happens to sit.

pieces.title: The weekly end-date suite runs once, in one file, instead of twice in two
pieces.why: Ten weekly end-bound tests exist in both weekly-end-date.test.ts and custom-spreadsheet.test.ts, so every one of them runs twice on every test run — 338 lines of tests that arrived on `main` through a merge conflict resolution rather than through any reviewed change.
pieces.context:
One surface, two files. What a person sees: nothing directly; this is the unit suite's runtime and the size of the diff a reviewer is asked to judge. What the contract is: no contract; this is a decision about which file owns the weekly end-bound suite.

I verified the duplication against `main` today rather than taking the epic's word for it. `weekly-end-date.test.ts` is 338 lines with 10 `it(...)`; `custom-spreadsheet.test.ts` is 1100 lines and carries all 10 of those titles, under the describes `weekly custom report end bound` (7) and `weekly grouped report end bound` (3). The bodies differ only by a `weeklyProps({...})` wrapper supplying the defaults `runCustom` already defaults to. The file entered via merge commit 9c44b8d as a conflict resolution that moved the suite out, while `b593293` — already an ancestor of `main` — left the originals in place. So it is a copy, not a move, and nothing was lost from custom-spreadsheet.test.ts.

That makes the decision narrow: delete the file, or fold back whatever it uniquely adds. Establish which by diffing the two suites before deleting anything; if the 338-line file contributes a case the 1100-line one lacks, that case moves and the file still goes. If it turns out to be genuinely load-bearing, say so in the PR rather than deleting it — the epic flags this as a judgement call and it is one.
acceptance: **AC-1** Each of the ten weekly end-bound test cases runs exactly once across the suite — after this, no two files execute the same case, and the suite's reportable test count drops by ten.

**AC-2** Whatever weekly-end-date.test.ts uniquely adds to the suite, if anything, is present in the surviving file before the 338-line file is deleted; if it adds nothing unique, it is deleted outright.
**AC-3** The decision is recorded in the pull request: the two suites were compared and the conclusion stated, so the next person reading this does not have to redo the comparison.
**AC-4** No test loses coverage in the process — every case that ran before still runs afterwards, by the same name, in the file that survives.
**AC-5** The remaining suite passes, with the same results it gave before this change apart from the ten duplicate runs no longer appearing.

pieces.title: A custom report's three synthetic rows get distinct React keys, and its console stays clean
pieces.why: Turning on 'Show empty rows' on a custom report makes React log a duplicate-key warning on every render, because Uncategorized, Transfers and Off budget are all declared with the empty id and the table keys each row by that id. The console noise makes every other warning on that screen unreadable.
pieces.context:
One surface, two files. What a person sees: Reports → Custom Report, Mode=Total, Viz=Data Table, with 'Show empty rows' enabled in Options. React logs "Encountered two children with the same key" on the report render, before any filter is applied; always reproducible. What the contract is: no new contract — the category list's shape is consumed by other code.

Verified in the tree: `categoryLists` in packages/desktop-client/src/components/reports/ReportOptions.ts appends `uncategorizedCategory` (line 348), `transferCategory` (354) and `offBudgetCategory` (360), all declared `id: ''`, and `categoryLists` returns all three (lines 398-401). `ReportTableList` at packages/desktop-client/src/components/reports/graphs/tableGraph/ReportTableList.tsx:77 renders each with `key={category.id}`.

**Risk, and this is the whole risk.** `id: ''` is load-bearing. It is how the query layer and the filters identify these rows, `CategorySelector` keys on `category.id` too (CategorySelector.tsx:226), and `uncategorized_id` is the field that actually distinguishes the three. Changing the `id` to make keys unique can break a lookup somewhere that matches on `''`. Prefer fixing the key at the render site over rewriting three entity identities; if you do change the ids, say which lookups you checked.
acceptance: **AC-1** Opening a Custom report with 'Show empty rows' enabled and no filter applied logs no React duplicate-key warning; the console is clean on the report render.
**AC-2** Uncategorized, Transfers and Off budget each still render as their own row, with their own amounts, exactly as they do today — the fix changes the key, not the rows.
**AC-3** Turning a filter on and off still narrows and restores those three rows correctly, so nothing that matches on the empty id has been broken by the key change.

**AC-4** Any `id` value introduced to make the keys distinct does not change what the category selector sends to the query layer, verified by the report still fetching and filtering correctly with all three rows enabled.
**AC-5** A test asserts the three synthetic rows render with three distinct keys, so the warning cannot come back unnoticed.

pieces.title: The shipped custom-report fix gets the release note the repository requires
pieces.why: PR #9 fixed a user-visible report bug and merged with no entry in `upcoming-release-notes/`, so the fix is absent from the release notes it should appear in. The repository requires a note for every user-facing change and the pull-request template carries the checklist item.
pieces.context:
One surface, one file. What a person sees: the release notes for the next Actual release, which today do not mention this fix. What the contract is: the release-note front matter — `category: Bugfix`, `authors:` entries that are people.

Verified against `main`: commit 026f8b6 (the squash of PR #9) touches 11 files and none of them is under `upcoming-release-notes/`; `upcoming-release-notes/` holds 92 notes from earlier work and none describes this fix. The change is user-visible — it fixes 'show empty rows' ignoring unchecked categories — so the category is `Bugfix`.

Name the file with a short descriptive slug rather than a number, per the convention in `upcoming-release-notes/`. Run `yarn generate:release-notes` if it is the supported path, or write the file by hand with the front matter above. packages/docs/docs/contributing/index.md:105 states the requirement.
acceptance: **AC-1** `upcoming-release-notes/` contains one new note describing the custom-report 'show empty rows' fix, named with a short descriptive slug rather than a number.
**AC-2** The note's front matter is `category: Bugfix`, and any `authors:` entry names a person.
**AC-3** The note's text describes what a user sees change — that 'Show empty rows' no longer drops the categories that were unchecked — rather than describing the implementation.
**AC-4** The repository's release-notes check accepts the note: run it and show it passing.

deferred.what: PR #9's title lacks the mandatory `[AI]` prefix and misspells 'categories'; its body does not use the repository's pull-request template and its '## Changed' section names 5 of the 11 files the pull request touched.
deferred.why: PR #9 is merged and its squash commit already carries the misspelled subject, so nothing here is a change to this repository that a work order can make. #75 is the canonical home for the `[AI]` prefix finding and is already open; re-filing it here would race it. The roadmap records that the available remedy is twelve `gh pr edit --title` calls and that this is a person's decision, not a ticket's — and the same roadmap notes #75 is currently parked behind a `sdlc:blocked` label that does not apply to it. Unblocked by a person, not by a piece.
